title: Reverse Win
reviewNotes: Three branches, 18 exact positions from the complete seven-piece root: White Kc1/Be7/c2 against Ka1/Rf7/Bd1/a2. Bd6 ...Rf5 Bb4 ...Rf3 Bc5 ...Rf4 Ba3 ...Bxc2 Bb2 mate forces the rook off its flexible seventh-rank defenses. Premature Ba3/...Rb7 and Bb4/...Rc7 comparisons lose; b4 capture completion is independent.

So, most players with white here would just resign. But you see, that would be an incredible mistake because white has one of the most peculiar ways to actually win this game. The key is to be able to land to this square because from here, we'll be able to check and mate the king with the bishop. But as I said, we cannot achieve that because the rook is simply going to stop the threat. But we need to reverse engineer the win here. With this incredible reverse thought process, we can finally come up with the idea bishop D6. This is the only move that forces the black rook to stay on this line. Of course, the threat being bishop to E5 and checkmate. So now the rook will have to go to F5 and defend the checkmate like this. But now we can continue with our plan. Bishop B4. Black has played rook F3. Bishop C5. And finally the rook is forced to defend this checkmate threat from F4. We can finally run to A3. And the rook has no way to prevent the checkmate in any way possible. Bishop can try to take the pawn, but this is simply an incredible checkmate.
